segments.text: You are going to listen to a lecture about the relation of diet to health and disease.
First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Now, listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning and welcome all of you to today's lecture.
This is the first lecture of a series of lectures about the relation between diet, health and disease.
What I want to do in this series is to provide evidence which shows that diet, in addition
to supplying material growth for the maintenance of the body, as well as the necessary energy
for it to function, also contains two groups of substances.
One tends to produce pathological changes in ill health, and the other helps the body
to protect itself.
First, let's take a look at the history of the relation between food and disease.
This was initiated by two discoveries.
One was the work of Eichmann, who proved in 1897 that berry berry was due to the absence
from the diet of a substance found in many foods, especially in cereals.
The substance came to be known as anti-berry berry, or vitamin B1.
The other was the discovery of Holsten Froelich in 1907 that fresh foods, especially fruits
and vegetables, contained a substance in whose absence from the diet the disease known as
scurvy developed.
This substance is now known as the anti-scorbutic vitamin, or vitamin C.
Both of these discoveries led to not only the establishment of the etiology of berry-berry
and scurvy, but also a new angle of thought that dietetic constituents are essential
to the maintenance of health.
Indeed, they led to investigations which ultimately made it clear that many of the
commoner diseases of civilized man had a dietetic factor as a basis.
So, in order to supply evidence that common foods consumed by mankind include both protective
and harmful elements, I propose to refer to three practical problems.
First, the condition of the bones and teeth.
Second, degenerative changes in the central nervous system.
And last but not least,
the liability of human beings to infection.
Now, let's look at our first example
of how eating can affect your body.
In this case, bones and teeth.
All of you here may know that the most important factor
in producing well calcified bones and teeth is vitamin D.
No matter what you eat for your meal,
Assuming that they are all natural foods,
a sufficient amount of vitamin D
will ensure perfect calcification of bones and teeth,
even when the amount of calcium and phosphorus intake
is surprisingly low.
On the other hand, if the vitamin D intake is insufficient
and the body is not exposed to sunlight,
however much calcium and phosphorus you consume,
your bones and teeth will suffer decalcification.
However, there are occasions where the influence
calcium and phosphorus intake is of great importance. It's when the amount of
vitamin D you take is moderate but insufficient. The best example of this is
seen when the main food carrying vitamin D is butter. In this circumstance, the
addition of calcium salts results in great improvement of bones and teeth.
In short, imagine the relation of calcium to vitamin D, calcium and
phosphorus intake like this. High vitamin D intake plus low calcium and phosphorus intake
equals healthy bones and teeth. With moderate vitamin D intake the more calcium and phosphorus
intake the better. Very low vitamin D intake plus infinite calcium and phosphorus intake
still equals imperfect calcification of bones and teeth. So far I've only mentioned those
foods aid in calcification. However, there is one group of foods that is outstanding because it
interferes with the deposition of calcifying salt in bones and teeth. Those foods are cereals.
There is a wide difference between cereals in this respect. For instance, as far as animal
experiments are concerned, oatmeal is the worst of all examined, and white flour interferes least
with the calcifying process.
The thing is that oatmeal is far richer in calcium and phosphorus than white flour.
This means a greater deficiency of calcium and phosphorus can be brought about by diets
which actually contain more of these substances, so that an analysis of mineral intake may
be quite misleading.
This may well be to emphasize that the calcifying effect of vitamin D will always antagonize
the anti-calcifying effect of cereals. You can see that the African natives almost always
have well-calcified teeth. They are all white and shiny and evenly arranged in powerful,
well-grown jaws, despite the fact that their diets are largely composed of cereals. It's
because their skin is often unprotected from the sun's rays, which generate high amounts
of vitamin D. If a native adopts a European habit of clothing, especially in childhood,
then his bones and teeth may be as badly calcified as those of average Europeans.
On the other hand, when Europeans provide abundant vitamin D in the diets of their
children, they will grow up with healthy bones and teeth.
Now, we'll look at the relation between tooth decay and diet.
That is the end of part four.
You now have half a minute to check your answers.
That is the end of the listening test.
You now have 10 minutes to transfer your answers onto the answer sheet.
